title: OpenAI says Apple's trade secrets lawsuit is "aggressive and oddly personal"
gist: OpenAI publicly rebutted Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit over stolen hardware designs, calling it careless and oddly personal and disputing Apple's account of pre-suit contact. The underlying driver is mutual encroachment: OpenAI is building AI consumer devices after acquiring Jony Ive's io studio and hiring 400+ ex-Apple staff, while Apple has partnered with Google to rebuild Siri.

insights.claim: Apple filed a lawsuit last month alleging OpenAI stole hardware designs as OpenAI prepared to launch its own AI-focused consumer devices, converting a former partnership into open litigation.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Litigation between a platform owner and its former AI supplier signals the distribution partnership is over; model any Apple-OpenAI integration revenue as at risk.
insights.locator: The post marks the latest escalation

insights.claim: The relationship soured specifically after OpenAI acquired io, the design studio founded by former Apple design chief Sir Jony Ive, and then hired a string of Apple employees.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The acqui-hire of a rival's design lineage is the identifiable trigger; talent transactions in hardware design now carry litigation risk that should be priced into deal terms.
insights.locator: OpenAI and Apple had previously partnered

insights.claim: Apple alleges more than 400 of its former employees now work at OpenAI, quantifying a talent drain large enough to constitute a systemic knowledge-transfer claim rather than isolated poaching.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A 400-person migration is a capability transfer, not attrition; it is the strongest evidence that OpenAI can realistically field consumer hardware and the core of Apple's legal exposure argument.
insights.locator: Apple alleged in its lawsuit that more than 400

insights.claim: Both companies are simultaneously invading each other's core business, with OpenAI moving into consumer products while Apple has joined forces with Google to revamp Siri.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Mutual encroachment means the legal fight is a proxy for a product war; the Google-Siri tie-up is the more consequential commercial fact for model-vendor market share.
insights.quote: The dispute comes as the two companies encroach on each other’s territory, with OpenAI venturing into consumer products and Apple joining forces with Google to revamp its Siri voice assistant.
insights.locator: The dispute comes as the two companies encroach

insights.claim: Apple says it contacted OpenAI in February to warn of an internal trade-secrets investigation and received no response, a timeline OpenAI directly disputes.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Pre-suit notice is a live factual dispute that bears on willfulness and therefore on damages exposure — a discovery flashpoint worth tracking.
insights.locator: It said it had received no response from OpenAI

insights.claim: OpenAI claims Apple's lawyers emailed the wrong person after confusing two Asian last names and asserted a discussion with OpenAI's General Counsel that Apple now concedes never happened.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Conceded factual errors in a plaintiff's notice narrative weaken the case at the injunction stage, where the court weighs credibility on an expedited record.
insights.quote: emailed the wrong person after confusing two Asian last names

insights.claim: OpenAI says Apple told it that Apple was resolving any issues and then went silent for five months before filing suit, undercutting any claim of urgent, ongoing harm.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A five-month delay is the standard argument against irreparable harm in preliminary-injunction practice; it materially lowers the odds Apple's injunction is granted as filed.
insights.quote: We then heard nothing for five months until they sued.

themes.theme: Named individuals and the misappropriation theory

insights.claim: Apple names Chang Liu, a former employee on some of its most sensitive product development programs, alleging he accessed Apple trade secrets after leaving the company in January.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Post-departure access allegations are the strongest form of trade-secret claim because they are provable from logs; this is the count most likely to survive early motions.
insights.locator: Apple alleged in its lawsuit that Chang Liu

insights.claim: OpenAI counters that Apple's own employees contacted Liu and asked for his help locating the information at issue, a fact OpenAI says Apple only now admits.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: If Apple solicited the access it now calls theft, the misappropriation theory collapses on consent — the single most case-determinative disputed fact disclosed here.
insights.quote: and asked for his help to locate this information

insights.claim: Apple also named OpenAI chief hardware officer Tang Tan, accusing him of seeking proprietary information while interviewing Apple employees, putting an OpenAI C-level executive directly in the complaint.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Naming the chief hardware officer targets the leadership of OpenAI's device program specifically; an adverse ruling could constrain the person running the roadmap.
insights.locator: Apple also named in its lawsuit a second former employee

insights.claim: Apple sought a US preliminary injunction on Monday to bar former employees and OpenAI from accessing, using or disclosing its trade secrets, plus a separate motion to expedite discovery and compel depositions of Liu and Tan.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Expedited discovery plus injunction is the aggressive posture used to disrupt a competitor's product timeline; the near-term risk to OpenAI is schedule slippage on its device, not damages.
insights.locator: Apple on Monday sought a preliminary injunction

insights.claim: OpenAI chose to litigate in public with a same-evening blog post rather than respond only in filings, framing the injunction as based on false information and unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Public rebuttal from a company that depends on developer and enterprise trust indicates it views reputational contamination as the bigger threat than the legal outcome.
insights.quote: We do not have, nor want, any of their trade secrets
insights.locator: “We do not have, nor want, any of their trade secrets,”

insights.claim: OpenAI's rhetorical strategy is to praise Apple's historic reputation for detail and then argue the lawsuit falls short of it, attacking the filing's credibility rather than Apple's standing to sue.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Attacking execution rather than the underlying right suggests OpenAI expects the case to be narrowed on the facts, not dismissed on the law — a longer, discovery-heavy fight.
insights.quote: This careless, aggressive and oddly personal lawsuit sadly doesn’t live up to that reputation
insights.locator: Apple is one of the greatest companies of all time

insights.claim: Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on OpenAI's rebuttal, leaving OpenAI's version of the pre-suit contact unchallenged in the news cycle.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Silence from the plaintiff cedes the narrative round; watch for whether Apple's reply brief substantiates the disputed General Counsel conversation.
insights.locator: Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment
